rail.sub: The same file, followed from the EMCAD DAHAO screen onto a live machine and off it onto fabric. Every course is taught in this sequence.
rail.s1Caption: The design digitised in EMCAD DAHAO.
rail.s1Detail: It starts as a path, not a picture. In EMCAD DAHAO the design is built from stitch types, directions and sequence — decisions the machine will follow exactly, including the wrong ones.
rail.s2Caption: The same design running on the machine.
rail.s2Detail: The file goes onto a live production machine while you watch it stitch. This is where a design that looked right on screen either holds, or shows you exactly what it got wrong.
rail.s3Caption: The same design finished on fabric.
rail.s3Detail: What comes off the machine is the only opinion that counts. You learn to read the finished piece back to the file, and to change the file until the piece is right.

workflow.h2: Six stages between an idea and a garment.
workflow.sub: Most classes stop at stage three. The two that decide whether a design ships are 04 and 05 — reading a failed sample, and correcting the file instead of compensating at the machine.
workflow.s1d: Read artwork the way the trade reads it: technique, scale, material, and what the fabric will allow.
workflow.s2d: Build the file in EMCAD DAHAO — stitch types, underlay, density and the travel order the head will follow.
workflow.s3d: Frame, thread, tension and needle chosen for this cloth. Setup is where half of all faults are decided.
workflow.s4d: Run a sample and read it honestly: puckering, gaps, registration, thread breaks.
workflow.s5d: Fix the file, not the symptom. An operator who slows the head down ships the fault anyway.
workflow.s6d: Run the job, finish the piece, and know why it came out right.
workflow.note: Every course teaches all six stages for its technique. That is the difference between learning a machine and learning the work.

problems.h2: The problems we teach you to solve.
problems.sub: If you already run a machine, you have met most of these. Each one has a cause, and the cause is teachable.
problems.p1c: Needle, thread and material are not matched — and the tension is set for a different cloth. Learn the combinations before you learn the machine.
problems.p2f: It looks right on screen and fails on fabric.
problems.p2c: Density, underlay and path direction. A design is not finished when it looks good; it is finished when it survives the cloth.
problems.p3f: Sequence and beadwork land out of register.
problems.p3c: Framing, travel order and correction. The hoop moves — the file has to be built expecting it.
problems.p4f: The operator compensates for a bad file.
problems.p4c: Slowing the head down ships the fault anyway. Fix it upstream, in the digitising, and it stays fixed for every run.
problems.p5f: Production is too slow to be worth it.
problems.p5c: Stitch count, colour changes and trims are design decisions. A better file runs faster on the same machine.
problems.p6f: Every machine on the floor is set up differently.
problems.p6c: Frame, stabiliser, needle and tension are decisions, not defaults. Set the machine for the cloth in front of you and the same file runs the same way on any head.

machineProof.h2: What a first stitch-out actually looks like.
machineProof.sub: Every institute shows you finished work. Here is the part they leave out: the same motif, stitched badly, with the four faults marked and the file change that fixes each one.
machineProof.fileNote: The design as it leaves EMCAD DAHAO: outline, control points and colour blocks. Nothing here has met cloth yet.
machineProof.failedNote: Puckered ground, a thin and gapping fill, the inner line out of register, and a broken thread. Four faults, four different causes.
machineProof.fixNote: Underlay added, density raised, travel order re-cut. Every change is made in the file — not by slowing the machine down.
machineProof.finalNote: The same design, run again. Clean satin, the echo in register, and a piece you would put your name on.
machineProof.foot: These are drawn diagrams of ordinary production faults, not a record of any student's work. Real studio and student photography is being shot.

coursesPage.title: Eleven techniques, taught on the machines that make them.
coursesPage.intro: Three families: machine embroidery, the modern techniques, and the EMCAD DAHAO design software behind both. Start wherever you are — most students arrive having never touched a machine.

pathway.line: The courses connect. Most students start at one machine technique, add EMCAD DAHAO design, and move into production work or a unit of their own.

stages.d: Frames, tension, threading and material — the part that stops your stitches breaking.
Zardosi, 4-beads, sequence, coding or chain and multi. Depth in one before breadth across many.
Make the files the machines run. This is the step that turns an operator into a designer.
Job work, a studio floor, or your own machines and your own clients.

relate.h2: How the three families fit together.
relate.line: They are not three separate schools. A machine technique gives you the hands, the design software gives you control over what the machine is asked to do, and the modern techniques sell alongside both.

points.d: Underlay, density and stitch direction are decided the same way in every machine technique. Learn them once and every other course reads faster.

points.t: The machine techniques are the trade
points.d: Zardosi, beads, sequence, coding, chain and multi are what Surat's units order every day, and each has its own faults to learn.
An operator runs someone's file. A digitiser decides whether the job works before the machine is switched on — and can take digitising work on its own.

points.t: Laser and tufting open other buyers
points.d: Cut-work and tufted pieces sell to boutiques, interior work and gifting, which is a different order book from garment job work.

signatures.zardosi-machine-embroidery: A tight parallel satin field with one restrained zari highlight — metallic thread laid in relief, stitch beside stitch.
signatures.flat-embroidery: A precise running field with clean, deliberate direction changes. Every other machine technique is written in this vocabulary.
signatures.four-beads-machine-work: Bead nodes attaching to a path, one after another, in the order the file sets.
signatures.sequence-work: Overlapping perforated discs, each caught through its centre, with one restrained reflective shift.
signatures.coding-cording-machine: A thicker cord following one curved Bezier path — the cord has weight the stitch line does not.
signatures.chain-multi-machine: Linked loop construction over a second line of rhythm: one loop pulled through the last, repeated in register.
signatures.applique-3d-embroidery: A raised border over a cut edge — the applied piece held down and the edge finished in one pass.
signatures.cross-stitch: A restrained crossing-stitch lattice, each cross the same size and the same direction.
signatures.laser-work: A precise trace, then one clean cut edge. No sparks and no scorching — a laser that behaves is a laser you have set correctly.
signatures.tufting: Loops rising from a baseline, each one to the same height, which is the whole difficulty.
signatures.emcad-embroidery-design: Vector nodes, then their handles, then the stitch path they produce. This is what digitising actually is.

servicesPage.sub: The studio side of Karma. Design development, digitizing and machine-ready files for your production — quoted by conversation, never by a price list that ignores what you are actually making.

chain.h2: Reference to machine-ready, in that order
chain.sub: Whatever you bring — a photograph, a physical sample, an old file that no longer runs — it goes through the same five stages. Nothing is quoted before we have seen it, and nothing ships before a sample has been stitched.
chain.s1Detail: A photograph, a swatch, a garment, an old file — or just a description. The first job is to work out what the piece actually is: technique, scale, ground, and what the cloth will allow. Send whatever you have; missing pieces are questions, not blockers.
chain.s2Detail: The design is rebuilt as stitch types, underlay, density, direction and travel order — not traced. A file built from a picture runs like a picture. This is where a design either becomes production-ready or inherits every fault the reference had.
chain.s3Detail: You see a stitched sample, on cloth, before the full run begins. On screen a design is an opinion; off the machine it is a fact, and that is the only version worth approving.
chain.s4Caption: The file changes, not the machine.
chain.s4Detail: Puckering, gaps, registration, thread breaks: each one is traced to the decision that caused it and fixed upstream in the file. Slowing the head down to hide a fault ships the fault anyway, on every run after this one.
chain.s5Caption: Yours, in the format your machine takes.
chain.s5Detail: Files, or finished production embroidery, whichever you came for. Tell us what your machine reads and what your deadline is — we will not guess either, and we do not publish a turnaround we have not agreed with you.

servicesPage.problemsSub: Nobody phones an embroidery studio asking for "digitising". They phone because something is not working, or because there is a look they cannot get made.
servicesPage.capabilitySub: The same eleven techniques the school teaches, on the same machines. This list is generated from the course catalogue, so it can never claim a technique the studio does not actually work in.
servicesPage.projectsSub: Generic project types, to show how a brief turns into something a machine can run.
servicesPage.projectsFoot: These are illustrative work types, marked as samples — not real commissions, and not an endorsement by any business. Real client work is published only with the client's permission.
servicesPage.turnaroundBody: It depends on the technique, the quantity and what is already on the floor, so we would rather agree a date with you than publish one that does not apply to your job. Tell us your deadline in the brief and we will say plainly whether it is workable.
servicesPage.formatsBody: Tell us the format your machine takes and we will deliver in it. If you are not sure, send the file you have or a photograph of the machine plate — that is usually enough to work it out.
servicesPage.talkSub: A five-minute call settles most briefs faster than a written one. You are also welcome to bring the sample to the studio and put it on a machine.

aboutPage.title: A studio that teaches, and a studio that ships.
aboutPage.intro: Karma is one floor in Mota Varachha doing two things with the same machines: training people who want the skill, and developing embroidery for businesses that need the work done. Neither side is a sideline.
aboutPage.twoSidesSub: This is the part most institutes cannot claim: the trainers are not between jobs, they are between orders.
aboutPage.academyBody: Eleven courses across machine embroidery, the modern techniques and EMCAD DAHAO design. Training happens at the machine from the first session, in Gujarati and Hindi, in morning and evening batches.
aboutPage.labBody: Design development, digitizing and production embroidery for garment businesses. The same machines, the same people, on live commercial work — which is why the teaching stays current.
aboutPage.machinesBody: Every technique taught on this floor, named. Swatches stand in for the studio photographs until the shoot happens — we would rather draw the stitch than borrow someone else’s picture of it.
aboutPage.storyTitle: The story, in the owner’s words
aboutPage.storySub: Three things on this page are the owner’s to say, not ours to write. They are marked, and they stay empty until we have them.
aboutPage.storyBody: The founding story goes here, in the owner’s own words: why Karma started, and what “from design screen to finished stitch” looks like on this floor every day.
aboutPage.karmaBody: What the name and the crown stand for, answered by the person who chose them.
aboutPage.trainersNote: Trainer profiles appear here with real names, photos and specialities once each is confirmed. No stand-ins, ever.
aboutPage.numbersNote: Only numbers we can stand behind. Counts come from the published catalogue; anything about students or ratings stays off this page until the owner has verified it in writing.
aboutPage.placeBody: Mota Varachha, Surat. Studio hours are open — you can walk in, see the machines running, and decide afterwards.
aboutPage.placeEntranceCaption: The entrance and signboard — what to look for from the road.
aboutPage.placeNote: Machines named by the technique they run. No head counts, speeds or model numbers until the studio supplies them.

storiesPage.title: What changed after the course?
storiesPage.sub: Named outcomes, published with consent: businesses started, jobs landed, rates raised.
storiesPage.consentBody: Every story here is shared with the student’s permission and verified by the studio before it goes up. Unverified entries stay marked as samples.
storiesPage.sampleBody: The six stories below are sample archetypes, written to show the shape a real story takes here — the routes people actually take into this trade. Each is marked as a sample and is replaced in place the moment a real, consented story is published. None of them claims an income, a job or a placement.
storiesPage.portraitsNote: Two frames, waiting for the studio shoot. A name goes under a portrait only once that person has given written consent — until then the frame says what it is waiting for and nothing about who is in it.
storiesPage.casesSub: Before, what was actually learned, and what they do now. A specific thing learned is worth more than any adjective about the institute.

cases.h2: Four faults, and what actually fixed them.
cases.sub: Case notes from the floor: the fault, what the sample told us, the setting that moved, and what the next run produced. This is what a trainer writes on a job card.
cases.foot: These are ordinary production faults with their ordinary causes — the same notes would be written in any embroidery unit in Surat. They describe technique, not any student's work, so there is nothing here about a person to verify.

notesPage.title: Notes from the machine floor.
notesPage.sub: Short answers to the questions that come up at the machine — why a sample failed, what to check, and which setting actually moved. Written by the people who run the machines, not by a marketing team.
notesPage.asideBody: Most of this already gets explained on Instagram, in Gujarati, standing next to a machine. It is good material trapped inside a video on somebody else's platform. These are the same answers in a form you can search, read on mobile data, and come back to.
notesPage.listSub: Each one is a question someone actually asked, with the answer first.
notesPage.exampleNote: Examples describe a fault and its fix. They are not a record of any student's or client's work.

notesPage.demoTitle: Easier to show than to write.
notesPage.demoBody: Bring the sample to a practical demo and put it on a machine. Ten minutes at the machine beats ten paragraphs.
